title: Perfect Pitch
objective: After this level you can explain perfect pitch and how rare it is.
summary: Absolute pitch, naming a note with no reference, is under 1 in 10,000 in the US and Europe, and far more common among Mandarin speakers who trained early. Most people use relative pitch.

cards.headline: Play a random note, and a few people can simply name it.
cards.body: No piano to check against, no starting note: they hear it and say "that's an A." It's called absolute pitch, or perfect pitch: naming or singing a note without any reference note. How rare is it, and why do some people have it?

cards.headline: Rarer than you'd think
cards.body: In the US and Europe, absolute pitch is estimated at fewer than 1 in 10,000 people. And it isn't a musical superpower. Having it doesn't necessarily make someone better at other musical tasks. A person with perfect pitch might hear Level 3's 440 Hz tone and instantly call it A, and still struggle with rhythm. It's a rare ear, not a guarantee.

cards.headline: What the rest of us use
cards.body: Remember Level 5? You recognize "Twinkle, Twinkle" starting on any note, because you hear the relationships between notes. That's relative pitch, and nearly everyone uses it. Even without perfect pitch, most people have a surprisingly accurate long-term memory for pitch, as long as they don't need to name the note. You may not know it's an A. You still remember how it sounds.

mascot.line: Don't mix these up: perfect pitch names a lone note; relative pitch hears the distances.

cards.headline: The language clue
cards.body: A 2006 study tested music students at the Central Conservatory in Beijing, who spoke Mandarin, and at the Eastman School in New York. In both, absolute pitch was more common the earlier training began. But at every starting age, it was far more common among the Mandarin speakers. In Mandarin, pitch changes meaning: "ma" can mean mother, hemp, horse or a scolding, depending on its tone.

questions.prompt: You don't have perfect pitch, yet you recognize "Twinkle, Twinkle" sung starting on any note. What are you using?

options.label: Absolute pitch, in a weaker form

options.label: Tempo, the speed of the beat
Relative pitch: the relationships between notes
Harmony: the chords underneath
